High-level ask for Acme: confirm which traffic profile (A: conversational triage, B: batch summarization, or C: hybrid) you want us to use as the canonical profile for cost modeling. Each profile changes the effective tokens-per-call and cache hit behaviour.

Key items we’ve flagged for MAP:
- Tokens-per-request baseline (prompt + completion) for each profile — drives tokens/$ and invoice estimates.
- Caching assumptions: percentage of prefix reuse after warmup (we estimate 20–40% savings for triage flows, less for summarization).
- Batching expectations: whether client is OK with ~50–150ms extra batching latency to get 2–4x GPU efficiency.
- Cold-start / cache-warmup plan for pilot day 1 traffic — avoids 3–4x transient token blowouts.

Proposed MAP milestone (tentative):
1) Today: agree canonical traffic profile and baseline tokens-per-call.
2) 2026-06-04: Redwood runs 48-hour synthetic eval (attached eval-plan-48h-traffic.json) to validate batching and cache numbers under your expected arrival curve.
3) 2026-06-11: Review results + update MAP with final tokens/$ and SLA notes.
4) 2026-06-18: Pilot sign-off & procurement handoff (DocuSign link to follow).

Can you confirm the traffic profile and whether procurement needs a separate packet for the unit economics? I can push a more formal MAP doc once we have your pick.

On Mon, Jun 1, 2026 at 09:12 AM Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai> wrote:
> Sara —

Quick technical notes to address Sara’s questions:

- Cache model: our default MAP assumes session-local prefix caching (per-tenant, per-model). That means repeated prefixes from the same patient/session hit the KV cache and avoid re-sending the prefix tokens to the model backend. Global caches across different patients are only enabled for explicit shared templates. In practice for triage flows we see 20–35% effective token savings after a warm period.

- Warmup dynamics: first 10–30 minutes of traffic can show a higher tokens-per-call due to cold KV misses; plan the MAP to either include a warmup window (recommended) or model the transient as a 2–3x cost delta for the first 100k requests.

- Batching vs latency: conservative numbers from our infra:
  * batching window 25ms (aggressive): 3–4x throughput improvement, P95/+30–50ms
  * batching window 100ms (safe): 1.6–2.2x throughput improvement, P95/+120–160ms
Given your 250ms P95 target, we can likely use a short window (25–50ms) on triage calls and still meet SLO. We’ll validate in the 48-hour run.

- Example econ (illustrative):
  * Avg tokens per raw call (prompt+completion): 420 tokens
  * Estimated cache savings (post-warm): 28% -> effective tokens/call = 302 tokens
  * If list price = $6.00 per 1M tokens (example): tokens per $ = ~166,667 tokens per $; effective calls per $ = ~166,667 / 302 ≈ 552 calls per $
  * Note: GPU amortization/instance-hour adds a small fixed component; in reserved/dedicated setups this shows up as a committed seat/throughput SKU rather than pure tokens.

Action items I’ll own for the eval: generate a traffic simulator with your real arrival curve, validate P95 vs batching window, and produce a sample invoice that splits raw tokens, cache credit, and a reserved throughput line. I’ll drop the outputs to the shared Drive link and attach a sample invoice PDF.

—Ben
